question_text: How many layers are defined in the standard ISO/IEC 7498-1 Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) reference model?
explanation: The standard OSI reference model defines exactly seven abstract layers: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, and Application.
learning_objective: Recall the structure of the OSI 7-layer model.

options.explanation: The OSI model consists of 7 hierarchical layers.
The TCP/IP model has 4 layers, whereas OSI has 7.
The hybrid pedagogical model often uses 5 layers, but OSI strictly defines 7.
No standard networking model defines 9 layers.

question_text: Which OSI layer is directly responsible for converting digital bits into physical signals (electrical voltages, light pulses, or radio waves)?
explanation: Layer 1 (Physical Layer) defines electrical, mechanical, optical, and timing specifications for transmitting raw bit streams over a physical communication medium.
learning_objective: Identify the role of OSI Layer 1.

options.explanation: The Physical layer encodes bits into physical media signals.
Data Link organizes bits into frames and handles local MAC addressing.
Network handles logical IP addressing and path routing.
Transport handles end-to-end process communication and segmentation.

question_text: What is the Protocol Data Unit (PDU) at the OSI Data Link layer (Layer 2)?
explanation: At Layer 2 (Data Link), the Protocol Data Unit is called a Frame. Frames encapsulate network packets and include header fields like source and destination MAC addresses.
learning_objective: Identify Layer 2 Protocol Data Units.

options.explanation: Layer 2 encapsulates packets into frames.
Packets are the PDU of Layer 3 (Network).
Segments are the PDU of Layer 4 (Transport).
Bits are the transmission unit of Layer 1 (Physical).

question_text: What is the Protocol Data Unit (PDU) at the OSI Network layer (Layer 3)?
explanation: At Layer 3 (Network), the Protocol Data Unit is called a Packet (or datagram). It contains source and destination logical IP addresses and routing control information.
learning_objective: Identify Layer 3 Protocol Data Units.

options.explanation: Layer 3 PDUs are packets (or datagrams).
Frames are Layer 2 PDUs.
Segments are Layer 4 PDUs.
Bits are Layer 1 units.

question_text: What is the Protocol Data Unit (PDU) at the OSI Transport layer (Layer 4) when using TCP?
explanation: At Layer 4 (Transport), data encapsulated with a TCP header is called a Segment. (When UDP is used, it is commonly called a Datagram).
learning_objective: Identify Layer 4 Protocol Data Units.

options.explanation: TCP PDUs at Layer 4 are known as segments.
Frames are Layer 2 PDUs.
Packets are Layer 3 PDUs.
Payload refers to the encapsulated data within a PDU.

question_text: Which OSI layer provides logical addressing (IP addresses) and path determination across interconnected networks?
explanation: Layer 3 (Network Layer) is responsible for logical addressing (IPv4/IPv6) and routing packets across intermediate routers to their ultimate destination network.
learning_objective: Define the primary role of the OSI Network layer.

options.explanation: Layer 3 handles logical IP addressing and routing.
Layer 2 uses physical MAC addresses within a single local segment.
Layer 4 uses port numbers to multiplex process communication.
Layer 5 manages session dialogues between applications.

question_text: Which OSI layer is responsible for establishing, maintaining, and synchronizing dialogues between two communicating applications?
explanation: Layer 5 (Session Layer) controls dialogues (connections) between computers, establishing, managing, and terminating sessions between local and remote applications.
learning_objective: Recall the function of the Session layer.

options.explanation: Session layer coordinates dialogue establishment and checkpointing.
Data link manages hop-to-hop frame transmission.
Network manages end-to-end packet delivery.
Physical layer transmits raw unstructured bit streams.

question_text: Which OSI layer handles data formatting, compression, and cryptographic encryption/decryption (such as ASCII, JPEG, and TLS presentations)?
explanation: Layer 6 (Presentation Layer) ensures that data passed from the application layer is formatted, translated, compressed, or encrypted into a standardized syntax the receiver can interpret.
learning_objective: Recall the responsibilities of the Presentation layer.

options.explanation: Presentation layer handles data representation, encryption, and compression.
Transport handles end-to-end transport and flow control.
Network handles packet forwarding and addressing.
Data Link handles frame delimiters and MAC media access.

question_text: Which OSI layer interfaces directly with end-user software applications (such as web browsers and email clients)?
explanation: Layer 7 (Application Layer) provides network services directly to software applications, hosting protocols like HTTP, DNS, SMTP, and SSH.
learning_objective: Identify the role of the Application layer.

options.explanation: Application layer protocols interact directly with software processes.
Physical layer deals with hardware cables and electrical signals.
Transport layer delivers data to port sockets, not directly to UI applications.
Data link layer interacts with network interface hardware.

question_text: What happens during the network encapsulation process as data travels DOWN the protocol stack from the sender?
explanation: As data travels down the stack, each lower layer adds its own protocol header (and sometimes trailer, like Layer 2 FCS) containing control information needed by that layer.
learning_objective: Explain the encapsulation mechanism.

options.option_text: Each layer prepends its own header containing metadata to the payload passed from the layer above
options.explanation: Encapsulation wraps higher-layer data with lower-layer headers.

options.option_text: Each layer strips away headers to make the packet as small as possible before transmission
options.explanation: Stripping headers is decapsulation, which occurs on the receiver.

options.option_text: The application data is permanently erased and replaced with random hex characters
options.explanation: Encapsulation preserves payload data intact inside headers.

options.option_text: All IP addresses are permanently converted into website domain names
options.explanation: Encapsulation adds protocol headers; it does not replace addresses with domain names.

question_text: What happens during the decapsulation process when a destination computer receives an incoming Ethernet frame?
explanation: Decapsulation occurs on the receiver: each layer unpacks the PDU, verifies the header for errors and addressing, strips that header off, and passes the remaining payload UP to the next higher layer.
learning_objective: Describe the decapsulation workflow on receiving endpoints.

options.option_text: Each layer inspects and removes its corresponding header, passing the unpackaged payload up to the layer above
options.explanation: Decapsulation unwraps headers progressively as data moves up to Layer 7.

options.option_text: The receiver adds three extra layers of encryption before saving the file to disk
options.explanation: Decapsulation removes transport and framing headers; it does not add encryption layers.

options.option_text: The frame is immediately broadcast out to every other host on the Internet
options.explanation: Unicast decapsulation is processed locally by the intended recipient host.

options.option_text: The receiver converts all IP addresses into MAC addresses
options.explanation: Decapsulation reads existing MAC and IP headers without altering them.

question_text: How many layers are in the original DARPA / DoD TCP/IP architectural model (RFC 1122)?
explanation: The standard TCP/IP model defines four layers: Network Access (Link), Internet, Transport (Host-to-Host), and Application.
learning_objective: State the number of layers in the TCP/IP model.

options.explanation: The TCP/IP model defines 4 layers: Link/Network Access, Internet, Transport, and Application.
7 layers corresponds to the OSI reference model.
TCP/IP has 4 layers.
6 layers does not correspond to standard networking models.

question_text: Which TCP/IP model layer corresponds to OSI Layer 3 (Network Layer)?
explanation: The Internet Layer of the TCP/IP model corresponds directly to Layer 3 (Network Layer) of the OSI model, hosting IP (IPv4/IPv6), ICMP, and ARP.
learning_objective: Map TCP/IP layers to OSI equivalents.

options.explanation: The TCP/IP Internet Layer performs the same role as OSI Layer 3 Network.
Network Access corresponds to OSI Layers 1 and 2.
Transport corresponds to OSI Layer 4.
Application corresponds to OSI Layers 5, 6, and 7.

question_text: Which OSI model layers are consolidated into the single 'Application' layer within the 4-layer TCP/IP model?
explanation: The TCP/IP Application layer encompasses the functionality of OSI Layers 5 (Session), 6 (Presentation), and 7 (Application).
learning_objective: Explain layer consolidation between OSI and TCP/IP.

options.explanation: TCP/IP consolidates OSI Layers 5, 6, and 7 into its Application layer.
Physical and Data Link are combined into the Network Access layer.
Internet and Transport are separate layers in TCP/IP.

options.option_text: Data Link, Network, and Transport layers
options.explanation: These represent separate functionalities across both models.

question_text: A technician troubleshoots network connectivity using the 'bottom-up' approach. Which component should be checked first?
explanation: Bottom-up troubleshooting begins at Layer 1 (Physical). The technician first checks physical cables, link indicator lights, power supplies, and transceiver connections before moving to higher layers.
learning_objective: Apply bottom-up troubleshooting methodology.

options.option_text: Physical cables, port link lights, and cable integrity
options.explanation: Bottom-up starts at Layer 1 Physical before checking IP addresses or applications.

options.option_text: The web browser cache and cookie settings
options.explanation: Checking web browser cache is a top-down application layer check.

options.option_text: DNS A records on the corporate authoritative nameserver
options.explanation: DNS checking is a higher-layer (Layer 7) troubleshooting step.

options.option_text: The user's Active Directory group policy permissions
options.explanation: User permissions represent an application/administrative layer issue.

question_text: A technician uses a 'top-down' troubleshooting approach for a user reporting that an internal website will not load. What should be verified first?
explanation: Top-down troubleshooting starts at Layer 7 (Application). The technician checks application-level configurations first (URL accuracy, web browser, application service status) before checking physical cables.
learning_objective: Apply top-down troubleshooting methodology.

options.option_text: The application configuration, URL spelling, and browser settings
options.explanation: Top-down starts at Layer 7 Application.

options.option_text: Whether the copper patch cable is seated properly in the wall jack
options.explanation: Checking the patch cable is a bottom-up Layer 1 check.

options.option_text: The electrical voltage running through the building conduit
options.explanation: That is an electrician's physical infrastructure test.

options.option_text: The router's BGP routing table entries
options.explanation: Checking BGP routing tables is an intermediate Layer 3 check.

question_text: At which OSI layer do port numbers (such as TCP port 80 or UDP port 53) function?
explanation: Port numbers are Layer 4 (Transport Layer) identifiers used by TCP and UDP to direct communication streams to the correct application process on a host.
learning_objective: Identify the layer where port numbers operate.

options.explanation: Port numbers reside in TCP and UDP headers at the Transport layer.
Data link uses MAC addresses.
Network layer uses IP addresses.
Physical layer operates on bits and signals.

question_text: Which OSI layer uses MAC (Media Access Control) addresses to direct traffic within a local broadcast domain?
explanation: MAC addresses are hardware-burned Layer 2 (Data Link Layer) addresses used by network interface cards (NICs) and switches to deliver frames across a local link.
learning_objective: Identify the layer of MAC addresses.

options.explanation: MAC addresses operate strictly at Layer 2 Data Link.
Layer 3 uses IP addresses.
Layer 4 uses port numbers.
Layer 7 uses domain names and URLs.

question_text: In OSI-based troubleshooting, what does the 'divide-and-conquer' approach involve?
explanation: Divide-and-conquer starts troubleshooting at the middle layer (usually Layer 3 Network by running a ping test). If ping succeeds, Layers 1-3 are verified, and the problem must be at Layers 4-7.
learning_objective: Explain the divide-and-conquer troubleshooting strategy.

options.option_text: Starting investigation at Layer 3 (e.g. testing with ping) to immediately isolate whether the issue is at lower layers (1-2) or upper layers (4-7)
options.explanation: Testing Layer 3 with ping effectively splits the 7 layers in half, saving diagnostic time.

options.option_text: Splitting the physical Ethernet cable in half with wire cutters to check copper purity
options.explanation: Severing cables destroys physical connectivity.

options.option_text: Assigning two technicians to yell at each other across the datacenter
options.explanation: This is not an engineering methodology.

options.option_text: Reinstalling the operating system before testing any network cables
options.explanation: Reinstalling OS is a drastic measure that should never precede basic diagnostics.

question_text: Which layer of the OSI model is responsible for flow control, windowing, and error recovery in reliable data delivery?
explanation: Layer 4 (Transport Layer), through protocols like TCP, provides end-to-end flow control (sliding windows), sequence numbers, acknowledgements, and retransmissions of dropped segments.
learning_objective: Identify Transport layer reliability mechanisms.

options.explanation: Transport layer manages flow control, sequence tracking, and error recovery.
Physical layer cannot detect or recover from dropped packets.
IPv4 and IPv6 are best-effort protocols without built-in reliability recovery.
Presentation formats and translates syntax.

question_text: What is the primary function of the Frame Check Sequence (FCS) located in an Ethernet frame trailer at Layer 2?
explanation: The Frame Check Sequence (FCS) uses a Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC-32) algorithm to detect whether any bits in the frame were corrupted during physical transmission over the wire.
learning_objective: Explain the purpose of the Frame Check Sequence.

options.option_text: To detect bit-level data corruption that occurred during physical transmission
options.explanation: FCS checks for transmission corruption; corrupted frames are discarded.

options.option_text: To encrypt the payload using a symmetric cryptographic key
options.explanation: FCS is an error-detecting checksum, not an encryption cipher.

options.option_text: To inform Google Analytics of the user's geographical location
options.explanation: Ethernet trailers have no connection to web marketing analytics.

options.option_text: To accelerate the electrical signal to twice the speed of light
options.explanation: Electrical signals cannot exceed the speed of light in the transmission medium.

question_text: Which protocol functions at the Internet layer of the TCP/IP model?
explanation: Internet Protocol (IP), along with ICMP and ARP, operates at the Internet layer of the TCP/IP model, handling logical addressing and routing.
learning_objective: Identify Internet layer protocols.

options.explanation: IP is the cornerstone protocol of the TCP/IP Internet layer.
TCP operates at the Transport layer.
SMTP operates at the Application layer.
Ethernet operates at the Link / Network Access layer.

question_text: Which protocol operates at the Transport layer of the TCP/IP model?
explanation: Both Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) and User Datagram Protocol (UDP) operate at the Transport layer of the TCP/IP model.
learning_objective: Identify Transport layer protocols.

options.explanation: UDP is a core Transport layer protocol.
HTTP operates at the Application layer.
ARP operates at the Link/Internet boundary.
IPv6 operates at the Internet layer.

question_text: What term describes the chunk of data generated by an application (Layer 7) before any network encapsulation occurs?
explanation: At the upper application layers (Layers 7, 6, 5), data is simply referred to as 'Data' or Application Data (Payload) prior to Transport layer segmentation.
learning_objective: Identify upper-layer data terminology.

options.explanation: At Layers 5-7, data is referred to generally as Data or Payload.
Frame is Layer 2 PDU.
Packet is Layer 3 PDU.
Bit is Layer 1 transmission unit.

question_text: Why does an Ethernet frame require both a header and a trailer, whereas IP packets only have a header?
explanation: Layer 2 frames require a trailer containing the Frame Check Sequence (FCS) so that receiving hardware can compute the CRC checksum over the entire frame contents as bits arrive.
learning_objective: Understand why Layer 2 incorporates a trailer.

options.option_text: The trailer contains the FCS checksum computed over the frame, allowing the receiver to verify data integrity upon receipt
options.explanation: Layer 2 puts the FCS in a trailer so it can be calculated on-the-fly during transmission.

options.option_text: The trailer contains the user's personal credit card information
options.explanation: Networking trailers contain protocol integrity metadata, never payment credentials.

options.option_text: IP packets are forbidden by RFC standards from detecting errors
options.explanation: IPv4 includes a header checksum, but Layer 2 validates the entire physical frame.

options.option_text: Ethernet cables can only carry data backwards
options.explanation: Ethernet transmission is sequential from preamble to trailer.

question_text: Which layer in the OSI model is responsible for assigning source and destination IP addresses?
explanation: The Network layer (Layer 3) adds source and destination logical IP addresses in its header during packet encapsulation.
learning_objective: Identify the layer responsible for IP addressing.

options.explanation: Source and destination IP addresses are added at Layer 3.
Data link adds MAC addresses.
Transport adds port numbers.
Session does not handle IP addressing.

question_text: Which OSI layer determines whether communication should be connection-oriented (reliable) or connectionless (unreliable)?
explanation: The Transport layer (Layer 4) selects between connection-oriented transport (TCP) or connectionless transport (UDP) depending on application requirements.
learning_objective: Understand Transport layer service modes.

options.explanation: Transport layer protocols determine connection-oriented vs connectionless modes.
Physical layer only transmits electrical/optical bits without connection awareness.
Data link deals with local media framing.
Presentation deals with data translation.

question_text: What is one key philosophical difference between the OSI reference model and the TCP/IP model?
explanation: The OSI model was designed as a theoretical, protocol-independent reference architecture before protocols were created. TCP/IP was developed practically around working protocols implemented in ARPANET/Unix.
learning_objective: Compare OSI and TCP/IP historical design philosophies.

options.option_text: OSI was designed as a theoretical reference model, whereas TCP/IP was built around working, implemented protocols
options.explanation: TCP/IP is pragmatic and protocol-specific; OSI is a formal conceptual framework.

options.option_text: OSI was designed for wireless smartphones; TCP/IP was designed for analog landline telephones
options.explanation: Both models predate modern smartphones by decades.

options.option_text: TCP/IP requires exactly seven layers; OSI has only four
options.explanation: TCP/IP has 4 layers; OSI has 7 layers.

options.option_text: OSI completely bans the use of routers and switches
options.explanation: OSI explicitly incorporates routing at Layer 3 and switching at Layer 2.

question_text: At which layer of the OSI model does an unmanaged Layer 1 repeater or electrical amplifier operate?
explanation: A repeater operates at Layer 1 (Physical). It regenerates and amplifies electrical or optical signals to overcome attenuation without reading frame headers or IP addresses.
learning_objective: Identify the operational layer of repeaters.

options.explanation: Repeaters regenerate raw physical signals at Layer 1.
Layer 2 devices (bridges/switches) inspect MAC frames.
Layer 3 devices (routers) inspect IP packets.
Layer 4 devices (firewalls) inspect transport ports.

question_text: When viewing an Ethernet frame captured on a wire, in what order do headers appear from outermost to innermost?
explanation: During transmission, lower-layer headers enclose higher-layer headers: Ethernet Header (Layer 2) comes first, followed by IP Header (Layer 3), then TCP/UDP Header (Layer 4), and finally the Application Data (Layer 7).
learning_objective: Trace header order in encapsulated frames.

options.option_text: Ethernet Header -> IP Header -> TCP Header -> Application Data
options.explanation: Outer encapsulation layer comes first on the wire: Layer 2 -> Layer 3 -> Layer 4 -> Payload.

options.option_text: Application Data -> TCP Header -> IP Header -> Ethernet Header
options.explanation: This is reverse order; the frame header arrives first on the wire.

options.option_text: IP Header -> Ethernet Header -> Application Data -> TCP Header
options.explanation: Ethernet header wraps the IP packet, so Ethernet header comes first.

options.option_text: TCP Header -> IP Header -> Ethernet Header -> Application Data
options.explanation: TCP is encapsulated inside IP, which is encapsulated inside Ethernet.
